panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Endoscopic patient image of lower esophagus with captioned circumferential black necrotic mucosa with friability, classic for acute esophageal necrosis. B: Endoscopic patient image of middle esophagus with captioned diffuse necrotic changes, consistent with acute esophageal necrosis; arrow annotation present. C: Retroflexed endoscopic patient image showing extension of necrotic injury to GE junction, attributed to acute esophageal necrosis in caption and article about acute esophageal necrosis.

panels.figure_caption: Esophagogastroduodenoscopy on hospital day 8 demonstrating acute esophageal necrosis. (A) Lower third of esophagus showing circumferential black, necrotic mucosa with friability and ulceration. (B) Middle third of esophagus with diffuse necrotic changes (arrow) and loss of normal vascular pattern. (C) Retroflexed view of the cardia demonstrating extension of necrotic injury to the gastroesophageal junction.

Repeat EGD on day 14 demonstrated healing esophageal ulceration and complete obstruction at the duodenal bulb apex (Figure 2). Computed tomography showed a distended, fluid-filled stomach with contrast failing to pass beyond the duodenal bulb (Figure 3). in_text_mentions: The images depict a case of necrotizing esophagitis in a 32-year-old man having ingested cocaine (Figures 1 and 2). Necrotizing esophagitis is rare and poorly understood. In elderly patients, it has been attributed to a combination of peptic injury exacerbated by gastric outlet obstruction and low flow ischemia (1), while in younger patients having ingested cocaine, it has been attributed to vasospasm (1,2). panels.rationale: Single diagnostic Day-1 upper GI endoscopy showing circumferential black necrotic distal esophageal mucosa with sharp GEJ demarcation, diagnostic of acute esophageal necrosis; real patient image with caption and in-text support for findings.
panels.attribution_text: Siddique et al. Black Esophagus: A Case of Acute Esophageal Necrosis in a Recovering Alcoholic.. Cureus 2025. doi:10.7759/cureus.98024. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Upper GI endoscopy performed on Day 1 Circumferential black necrotic mucosa of the distal esophagus, sharply demarcated at the gastroesophageal junction; findings diagnostic of acute necrotizing esophagitis (“black esophagus”)
in_text_mentions: Under sedation (midazolam 4 mg, fentanyl 100 µg), upper GI endoscopy revealed extensive circumferential black discoloration of the esophageal mucosa extending from approximately 20 cm from the incisors to the gastroesophageal junction, with a sharp demarcation to healthy gastric mucosa. The mucosa appeared friable and hemorrhagic but without active bleeding. Mild gastritis and duodenitis were also noted. The appearance was diagnostic of AEN (Figure 1). The procedure was terminated early due to tachycardia (170 bpm).

in_text_mentions: infusion. The endoscopic report revealed that, starting at 26 cm from the incisors, the entire circumference of the esophageal mucosa was covered with fibrinous exudates and areas of interstitial hemorrhage. The distal third exhibited black tissue compatible with necrosis, which terminated abruptly at the gastroesophageal junction at 39 cm (Figure 5). In the stomach, a sparse accumulation of coffee-ground fluid with remnants of old blood was observed, and the mucosa showed irregular erythema and petechial subepithelial punctate lesions, leading to the diagnosis of cardiogenic black esophagus.

panels.figure_caption: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy demonstrating diffuse circumferential black discoloration of the esophageal mucosa with extensive patchy necrotic involvement (blue arrow). The mucosa is markedly friable, with abundant adherent necrotic debris and complete obliteration of the normal vascular pattern. Direct contact with the endoscope reveals severely devitalized and easily deformable tissue (green arrow).
in_text_mentions: . The proximal third of the esophagus demonstrated friable mucosa with multiple punctate areas of submucosal hemorrhage. The middle and distal thirds exhibited extensive circumferential necrosis involving the entire esophageal mucosa, accompanied by multiple hemorrhagic areas covered with fibrin deposits (Figures 1, 2). Owing to the extensive necrosis observed, the marked tissue fragility, and the absence of feasible endoscopic therapeutic interventions, the procedure was terminated after approximately 10 minutes to minimize the risk of major complications, particularly esophageal perforation.

panels.figure_caption: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy demonstrating a sharp demarcation between necrotic esophageal mucosa (pink arrow) and adjacent viable mucosa (green arrow), a characteristic finding of acute esophageal necrosis. The necrotic process ends abruptly at the gastroesophageal junction, with preservation of the adjacent gastric mucosa.
in_text_mentions: . The proximal third of the esophagus demonstrated friable mucosa with multiple punctate areas of submucosal hemorrhage. The middle and distal thirds exhibited extensive circumferential necrosis involving the entire esophageal mucosa, accompanied by multiple hemorrhagic areas covered with fibrin deposits (Figures 1, 2). Owing to the extensive necrosis observed, the marked tissue fragility, and the absence of feasible endoscopic therapeutic interventions, the procedure was terminated after approximately 10 minutes to minimize the risk of major complications, particularly esophageal perforation.

hly characteristic of AEN. The presence of circumferential black discoloration, friable mucosa, submucosal hemorrhage, and fibrin deposits closely mirrors the descriptions reported by Okamoto et al. [5]. Furthermore, the abrupt transition between viable and necrotic mucosa identified in Figure 2 represents one of the classic endoscopic hallmarks of AEN originally described by Gurvits [7]. Due to the extensive necrosis and marked mucosal fragility observed during endoscopy, the procedure was terminated prematurely to minimize the risk of major complications, particularly esophageal perforation.

in_text_mentions: An 84-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with a 3-week history of hoarseness and decreased appetite. Four weeks before admission, she had started to take prednisolone (30 mg/day) for her unilateral facial palsy. On arrival, she was obtunded and her systolic blood pressure was 80 mmHg. Bowel sounds were reduced, and abdominal X-ray revealed gastric and small intestinal expansion. No evidence of intestinal obstruction was obtained. The upper endoscopy revealed necrotic esophagitis in the middle and lower parts of the esophagus and duodenal erosions (Figure 1).

panels.figure_caption: Black appearance of the esophagus in the middle third of the esophagus
in_text_mentions: Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) revealed severe mucosal changes in the middle and lower one-third of the esophagus, characterized by black discoloration (Figures 1 and 2), LA grade D esophagitis (Figure 3), normal stomach (Figure 4), mild erosions in the duodenal bulb (Figure 5), and a normal-appearing second portion of the duodenum with the patent CBD stent placed during recent ERCP (Figure 6). These esophageal findings were highly suspicious for acute esophageal necrosis and were not present during the recent ERCP performed three weeks ago.

in_text_mentions: odenoscopy (EGD) was performed and demonstrated a functional obstruction encountered in the upper third of the esophagus (Figure 4). Gentle passage of the endoscope relieved the resistance, consistent with reduction of volvulus-related obstruction. Diffuse, circumferential black discoloration of the esophageal mucosa consistent with AEN, extending from the distal esophagus proximally to the proximal/upper third (Figure 5). A large paraesophageal hernia with distorted gastric anatomy and scattered erosions (Figure 6), and two clean-based duodenal bulb ulcers without stigmata of active bleeding.

in_text_mentions: Histopathological examination of the esophageal biopsy revealed edematous and necrotic tissue infiltrated by neutrophils and macrophages, with loss of the mucosal lining. A fragmented and necrotic muscularis layer was also noted, consistent with acute esophageal necrosis. Duodenal biopsy showed focal erosion with degenerating epithelial cells and neutrophilic infiltrates. The lamina propria was edematous and infiltrated by lymphocytes and eosinophils, consistent with acute duodenitis (Figure 3).
